question: Think of a research study design as a map or plan. What is its main job?

options.A: To act as a blueprint for answering a clinical question
options.B: To write the final conclusion of the research paper
options.C: To calculate the total budget needed for the project
options.D: To recruit patients for clinical drug trials

explanation: Great job! Just like building a house needs a drawing, a study design is your step-by-step plan for gathering and checking your information. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h1)

question: Why do nurses care about picking a good, solid study design?

options.A: It guarantees that funding will be approved by the hospital board
options.B: It allows the researcher to skip the ethical review process entirely
options.C: It ensures the resulting evidence is strong enough to guide safe patient care
options.D: It eliminates the need for any statistical analysis in the project

explanation: Spot on! We want to base our bedside nursing on facts we can truly trust to keep our patients safe and healthy. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h1)

question: When a researcher is doing a quantitative study, what are they mainly looking at?
explanation: You got it! Quantitative research is all about the numbers, measurements, and stats. Think 'Quantity = Numbers'! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h2)

question: A nurse wants to understand the deep feelings and experiences of mothers going through postpartum depression. Which study style fits best?
explanation: Brilliant! When you want to hear people's stories and feelings in their own words, qualitative research is your go-to choice. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h2)

question: What is the big giveaway that a study is observational?

options.A: Patients are given a new medication to test its safety
options.B: The researcher does not apply any experimental intervention
options.C: Data is collected exclusively through laboratory blood tests
options.D: All participants must be followed up for at least ten years

explanation: Exactly! In observational studies, researchers just sit back, watch, and record what happens naturally without interfering. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h3)

question: Which study style looks backward in time, comparing people with a sickness to healthy folks?
explanation: Spot on! Case-control studies take people who already have the 'case' and look back at their past to compare with healthy controls. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h3)

question: What is the main thing that separates a true experiment from a quasi-experiment?

options.A: Avoiding all forms of statistical testing
options.B: The use of patient interviews for data collection
options.C: The presence of a clinical nurse researcher
options.D: Random assignment of participants to groups

explanation: You nailed it! True experiments use random chance (like flipping a coin) to drop people into different groups, while quasi-experiments don't use strict random mixing. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h4)

question: A nurse wants to test a new handwashing style on two hospital wards without disrupting how the wards are already set up. What is the best study type?
explanation: Correct! When you can't randomly mix up individual patients because of real-world ward setups, a quasi-experimental design saves the day. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h4)

question: Why would a researcher choose to observe heavy drinkers instead of forcing an experiment where people drink alcohol for years?

options.A: Alcohol abuse is too rare to study in a clinical trial setting
options.B: Experimental trials cannot use statistical analysis
options.C: Observational studies are much more expensive to conduct
options.D: It is unethical to force participants to consume alcohol for an experiment

explanation: Well reasoned! We can never intentionally put people in harm's way or force them to take harmful substances just for an experiment. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h5)

question: When deciding on a study design, which of these is completely irrelevant?

options.C: The specific research question being asked
options.D: The personal favorite color of the lead researcher

explanation: Haha, exactly! A researcher's favorite color has zero to do with science. Decisions are based purely on safety, questions, and resources. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h5)

question: Which group of people needs extra protection and care in nursing research?
explanation: Spot on! Children, prisoners, and unconscious patients need extra ethical safeguards because they might not be fully free to say yes or no. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h6)

question: Why might an ethics committee step in and halt a clinical trial early?

options.A: All participants have decided to change their personal lifestyles
options.B: The research team has run out of interesting topics to write about
options.C: The hospital building requires routine maintenance
options.D: The experimental treatment is proven to be overwhelmingly beneficial

explanation: Wonderful logic! If a new treatment turns out to be a life-saver early on, researchers stop the trial so everyone else can benefit right away. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h6)

question: What is the main drawback of using a quick survey (cross-sectional study) to prove cause and effect?

options.A: Cross-sectional surveys only capture data at one single point in time
options.B: Surveys are always illegal to conduct inside modern hospitals
options.C: Statistical software cannot process survey data
options.D: Participants never answer survey questions honestly

explanation: You got it! Because a survey takes a snapshot at just one moment, you can't tell which came first—the cause or the effect. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h7)
